hubs.note: Know how you learn, what you believe, and where your gaps are. “Know thyself” was carved at the temple of Apollo at Delphi, and Socrates made it the starting point of philosophy.

Theory and action together: learn by doing real work, then reflect on it. Aristotle set praxis, thoughtful action, beside theory. Paulo Freire defined it as reflection and action upon the world in order to transform it.
Knowledge open to everyone, and fields connected into a whole. The word university comes from the Latin universitas: the whole community of teachers and scholars.
Knowledge free to read and reuse: open articles, open data, open courses and open tools, so that anyone can learn and build on what is known.
Shared hubs where labs, schools and communities in one field work together and connect across fields, joined into one network.
Continents, vegetation, climate, and human migration layered across 540 million years. The first hub in this network.
Animals wild and in human care: how they live, perceive, are classified, and share places with people.
Birds, the living dinosaurs: their evolution, ecology, color, song and care.

Ice cores, ocean sediments, and tree rings that record past temperature and rainfall. Who would contribute: Climate science groups; Public climate data archives. A student could start with: Has this place ever been as warm as it may become by 2100? From the Drifting Through Deep Time example network on The Open Commons of Learning.

Genetic evidence of how populations split, mixed, and moved. Who would contribute: Genomics labs. A student could start with: What does ancient DNA agree with, or contradict, in the archaeological record? From the Drifting Through Deep Time example network on The Open Commons of Learning.

How the deep past informs what we protect and restore today. Who would contribute: Conservation groups; Restoration ecologists. A student could start with: Which plants that grew here before could help restore it now? From the Drifting Through Deep Time example network on The Open Commons of Learning.

Teachers, museums, and video creators who make deep time understandable. Who would contribute: Science communicators; Museum educators; Teachers. A student could start with: What's the clearest way to show 500 million years on one screen? From the Drifting Through Deep Time example network on The Open Commons of Learning.

Language families as another trace of how people spread. Who would contribute: Linguistics departments. A student could start with: Do word families for plants and animals follow the migration routes? From the Drifting Through Deep Time example network on The Open Commons of Learning.

How people moved across continents, and how land bridges, coastlines, and climate shaped their routes. Who would contribute: Anthropologists and archaeologists; Population geneticists; Community historians. A student could start with: Which routes could people have taken into this region, and when were they open? From the Drifting Through Deep Time example network on The Open Commons of Learning.

Flood stories, origin myths, and dream imagery that may hold memories of changing landscapes. Who would contribute: Folklorists; Psychologists of dreams and memory. A student could start with: Could a flood myth preserve a real sea-level rise? From the Drifting Through Deep Time example network on The Open Commons of Learning.

Knowledge held by communities and elders about land, plants, and change, shared on their terms. Who would contribute: Community knowledge keepers; Oral history projects. A student could start with: What do local elders remember about how the land has changed? From the Drifting Through Deep Time example network on The Open Commons of Learning.

How people experience and imagine spans of time far beyond a human life. Who would contribute: Philosophy departments. A student could start with: What does it feel like to stand on rock 400 million years old? From the Drifting Through Deep Time example network on The Open Commons of Learning.

What past climate shifts suggest about the decisions in front of us. Who would contribute: Policy researchers; Public agencies. A student could start with: What does the deep past say about how fast ecosystems can adapt? From the Drifting Through Deep Time example network on The Open Commons of Learning.

Reconstructions of moving continents, opening oceans, and rising mountains. Who would contribute: Geophysics labs; Open plate-reconstruction datasets; Geology educators and YouTube science communicators. A student could start with: When did your region last share a coastline with another continent? From the Drifting Through Deep Time example network on The Open Commons of Learning.

Fossil pollen and plant records that show which forests and grasslands grew where. Who would contribute: Palynology labs; Herbaria and museum collections; Volunteers sorting samples. A student could start with: How did the plants around here change at the end of the last ice age? From the Drifting Through Deep Time example network on The Open Commons of Learning.

A living library that gathers what people have recorded about parrots (scientific papers, veterinary case reports, avicultural journals, photographs, theses, citizen-science observations) and connects it while keeping every record's source and context. Founded and directed by EV Voltura, PhD (Texas A&M). Its work includes knowledge graphs, a history of parrot names since 1758, multilingual species names, a student-built cockatoo diet dataset, and a hyperspectral feather library. A participating node of The Open Commons of Learning.
Parrots, cockatoos, lories and their relatives, in the wild and in human care.
Avicultural bulletins, old books and records digitized and cataloged, because what gets preserved shapes the history future generations can read.
What parrots eat in the wild and in human care, recorded with the context needed to compare like with like.
Research that lets birds choose whether to take part, honesty about the costs of AI tools, and a future where humans and parrots coexist.
Hyperspectral imaging of feathers, including ultraviolet colors birds can see and people cannot.
Graphs that show where research is thick and where it is thin: maps of what has been published, not summaries of what is true. AI may help find links, reviewed by people.
hubs.t: Knowledge Graphs as Maps of the Literature

hubs.note: Veterinary and medical literature on parrots linked to diseases, drugs and diagnostics, with evidence grading in development.
Parrot names across languages and scripts, verified by native speakers, with community attribution respected.
Scientific names change; historical names are part of the record, not mistakes. A translation table between old literature and current checklists, keeping each authority's decision.
Every record keeps its citation and context: wild or captive, where, when, and how it was reported. Conflicting reports stay visible, and evidence is weighed by how it was obtained.
Researchers, veterinarians, aviculturists, caregivers, students and enthusiasts are all teachers here. Student research, volunteers, citizen science, and a norm of kindness.

Sites, tools, and settlements that place people in a landscape. Who would contribute: Field schools; Regional museums. A student could start with: What can a single site tell us about the climate its people lived through? From the Drifting Through Deep Time example network on The Open Commons of Learning.

nodes.name: Socrates
nodes.desc: Taught by questioning. In Plato's account he said the unexamined life is not worth living.

nodes.name: Plato
nodes.desc: Student of Socrates. Founded the Academy, where Aristotle studied for about twenty years.

nodes.name: Aristotle
nodes.desc: Founded the Lyceum. Set praxis, thoughtful action, beside theory, and studied animals and nature firsthand.

nodes.name: Theophrastus
nodes.desc: Aristotle's successor at the Lyceum. His Enquiry into Plants is one of the first systematic studies of plants.

nodes.name: The Lyceum
nodes.desc: Aristotle's school, built on conversation, shared collections of observations, and close mentorship.

nodes.name: Seneca
nodes.desc: Stoic philosopher who described reviewing each day before sleep.

nodes.name: Wilhelm von Humboldt
nodes.desc: Shaped the founding of the University of Berlin around the unity of research and teaching.

nodes.name: Alexander von Humboldt
nodes.desc: Naturalist who saw nature as one interconnected whole. His Kosmos tried to describe all of it.

nodes.name: Humboldt University of Berlin
nodes.desc: Model for the modern research university, joining research and teaching.

nodes.name: John Dewey
nodes.desc: Learning by doing, with school as a real community. Lectured in China from 1919 to 1921.

nodes.name: Tao Xingzhi
nodes.desc: Studied with Dewey at Teachers College, Columbia. Championed teaching, learning, and doing as one, especially in rural education.

nodes.name: Lev Vygotsky
nodes.desc: Described the zone of proximal development: we learn best just beyond what we can do alone, with help.

nodes.name: Paulo Freire
nodes.desc: Pedagogy of the Oppressed. Defined praxis as reflection and action upon the world in order to transform it.

nodes.name: Myles Horton
nodes.desc: Founded Highlander after visiting Danish folk high schools. Co-wrote We Make the Road by Walking with Freire.

nodes.name: Highlander Folk School
nodes.desc: Adult education for the labor and civil rights movements, modeled partly on Danish folk schools.

nodes.name: N. F. S. Grundtvig
nodes.desc: Inspired the folk high school movement: learning for life, open to everyone.

nodes.name: Folk high schools
nodes.meta: Denmark and the Nordic countries · first in 1844 · Danish
nodes.desc: Residential schools with no exams, often a year between secondary school and university.

nodes.name: bell hooks
nodes.desc: Teaching to Transgress and engaged pedagogy. Drew deeply on Freire, whom she met.

nodes.name: Ivan Illich
nodes.meta: Austria and Mexico · 1926–2002 · Spanish, English, German
nodes.desc: Deschooling Society proposed open “learning webs” connecting learners with people and resources.

nodes.name: CIDOC
nodes.desc: Illich's center for open, cross-cultural seminars and learning.

nodes.name: Rabindranath Tagore
nodes.desc: Founded a school at Santiniketan where classes met outdoors. It grew into Visva-Bharati University.

nodes.name: Visva-Bharati

nodes.name: Mohandas K. Gandhi
nodes.desc: Proposed Nai Talim, education through productive craft and work.

nodes.name: Nai Talim
nodes.desc: “Basic education”: learning built around useful work and community life.

nodes.name: Julius Nyerere
nodes.desc: Called Mwalimu, “teacher.” His Education for Self-Reliance (1967) imagined schools as working farms and communities.

nodes.name: Manabu Sato
nodes.desc: Built “learning community” schools around collaborative learning, drawing on Dewey and Vygotsky.

nodes.name: Escuela Nueva
nodes.desc: Rural schools where students learn at their own pace, in groups, and teach one another.

nodes.name: Edmund Husserl
nodes.desc: Founded phenomenology, the careful study of experience as it is lived.

nodes.name: Maurice Merleau-Ponty
nodes.desc: Phenomenology of perception and the body, building on Husserl.

nodes.name: David Kolb
nodes.desc: The experiential learning cycle: do, reflect, generalize, try again.

nodes.name: Robin Wall Kimmerer
nodes.desc: Botanist whose Braiding Sweetgrass brings traditional ecological knowledge and science together.

nodes.name: Jean Lave
nodes.desc: Co-author of Situated Learning: newcomers learn by joining a community of practice.

nodes.name: Etienne Wenger
nodes.desc: Co-author of Situated Learning. Developed the idea of communities of practice.

nodes.name: Elinor Ostrom
nodes.desc: Nobel laureate who showed how communities govern shared resources, or commons.

nodes.name: Charlotte Hess

nodes.name: Susan Leigh Star

nodes.name: Timothy Gowers

nodes.name: Erich Fromm
nodes.meta: Germany, United States, and Mexico · 1900–1980 · German, English
nodes.desc: Psychoanalyst and social philosopher. Lived in Cuernavaca, where he was a friend of Illich, and wrote on freedom, love as a practiced art, and having versus being.

nodes.name: To Have or To Be?
nodes.desc: Contrasts the having mode, which possesses and consumes, with the being mode, which engages and shares. Includes students who collect lecture notes versus students who think along.

nodes.name: Nicomachean Ethics
nodes.desc: Virtue as a habit formed through practice, and the good life as activity guided by practical wisdom.

nodes.name: Robert M. Pirsig
nodes.desc: Writer and former teacher of rhetoric who experimented with withholding grades from his students.

nodes.name: Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance

nodes.desc: A motorcycle journey and an inquiry into Quality: caring about what you do, and joining hands-on and theoretical understanding.

nodes.name: Pedagogy of the Oppressed

nodes.name: Deschooling Society
nodes.desc: Argues for open learning webs: directories that connect people who want to learn with people and things to learn from.

nodes.name: Confucius
nodes.desc: Taught through conversation with students, whose record of his sayings became the Analects. Stressed lifelong learning and self-cultivation.

nodes.name: Ibn Sina (Avicenna)
nodes.meta: Persia and Central Asia · c. 980–1037 · Arabic and Persian
nodes.desc: Physician and philosopher whose encyclopedic works spanned medicine, logic, and natural philosophy, building on Aristotle.

nodes.name: Ibn Rushd (Averroes)
nodes.desc: Wrote extensive commentaries on Aristotle that shaped philosophy in both the Islamic world and medieval Europe.

nodes.name: Ibn Khaldun
nodes.desc: His Muqaddimah is an early work of history and social science, with reflections on how teaching should build skill gradually, through practice.

nodes.name: House of Wisdom
nodes.desc: A center where scholars translated Greek, Persian, and Indian works into Arabic, Aristotle among them.

nodes.name: Nalanda
nodes.desc: A great Buddhist center of learning that drew students and teachers from across Asia.

nodes.name: Al-Qarawiyyin
nodes.desc: Founded by Fatima al-Fihri, and often cited as one of the oldest continuously operating universities.

nodes.name: William James
nodes.desc: Psychologist and pragmatist philosopher of experience and attention. An influence on Dewey, Husserl, and Nishida.

nodes.name: Kitarō Nishida
nodes.desc: Founder of the Kyoto School. His An Inquiry into the Good begins from “pure experience,” drawing on William James and Zen.

nodes.name: Thich Nhat Hanh
nodes.desc: Zen teacher of mindfulness and engaged Buddhism, whom bell hooks named as one of her teachers.

nodes.name: Jiddu Krishnamurti
nodes.desc: Spoke of education as freedom and self-understanding, and founded schools in India and England, among them Rishi Valley.

nodes.name: Simone Weil
nodes.desc: Her essay on the right use of school studies argues that the deepest purpose of study is learning to pay attention.

nodes.name: Hannah Arendt
nodes.meta: Germany and United States · 1906–1975 · German, English
nodes.desc: Her essay “The Crisis in Education” argues that teachers carry the responsibility of introducing the young to a shared world.

nodes.name: Martha Nussbaum
nodes.desc: Aristotle scholar whose Not for Profit argues that democracies need the humanities and critical thinking.

nodes.name: Kwasi Wiredu
nodes.desc: Called for “conceptual decolonization”: rethinking philosophical ideas through African languages and traditions.

nodes.name: Franz Boas
nodes.meta: Germany and United States · 1858–1942 · German, English
nodes.desc: Founder of American cultural anthropology, who trained a generation of students at Columbia.

nodes.name: Ruth Benedict
nodes.desc: Boas's student and colleague, author of Patterns of Culture, and mentor to Margaret Mead.

nodes.name: Margaret Mead
nodes.desc: Studied how young people learn their cultures, beginning with Coming of Age in Samoa.

nodes.name: Gregory Bateson
nodes.meta: United Kingdom and United States · 1904–1980 · English
nodes.desc: Steps to an Ecology of Mind described levels of learning, including learning how to learn.

nodes.name: Zora Neale Hurston
nodes.desc: Novelist and anthropologist who studied with Boas and collected folklore across the American South and the Caribbean.

nodes.name: Bronisław Malinowski
nodes.meta: Poland and United Kingdom · 1884–1942 · Polish, English
nodes.desc: Made long-term participant observation, living within a community, the core of anthropological fieldwork.

nodes.name: Claude Lévi-Strauss
nodes.desc: The Savage Mind describes the “science of the concrete” in traditional knowledge, rigorous in its own right.

nodes.name: Clifford Geertz
nodes.desc: Called for “thick description”: understanding actions through the meanings they hold for the people involved.

nodes.name: Barbara Rogoff
nodes.desc: Studies how children learn by observing and pitching in to the work of their communities, especially in Indigenous communities of the Americas.

nodes.name: Tim Ingold
nodes.desc: His Making and Anthropology and/as Education argue that learning happens through attentive practice in the world.

nodes.name: Anna Tsing
nodes.desc: The Mushroom at the End of the World follows matsutake through forests and markets: a model of collaborative, multispecies research.

nodes.name: Eduardo Viveiros de Castro
nodes.desc: Described Amerindian perspectivism, treating Indigenous thought seriously as philosophy.

nodes.name: Linda Tuhiwai Smith
nodes.meta: Aotearoa New Zealand · Māori scholar · English, Māori
nodes.desc: Decolonizing Methodologies (1999) sets out how research can respect and serve Indigenous communities.

nodes.name: Laozi
nodes.desc: The Tao Te Ching, attributed to him, teaches knowing oneself and acting in harmony with the way of things.

nodes.name: The Buddha
nodes.meta: South Asia · c. 5th century BCE · Pali and Sanskrit traditions
nodes.desc: Taught that insight comes from close, patient attention to one's own mind and experience.

nodes.name: Al-Ghazali
nodes.desc: His Deliverance from Error recounts a scholar's search for certainty through honest self-examination.

nodes.name: Michel de Montaigne
nodes.desc: Invented the essay as a way of testing and knowing oneself. His essay on educating children favors judgment over memorization.

nodes.name: Plum Village
nodes.desc: Thich Nhat Hanh's practice community, where mindfulness is learned by living it together.

nodes.name: Rishi Valley School
nodes.desc: A school founded by Krishnamurti around self-understanding, nature, and learning without fear.

nodes.name: Maria Montessori
nodes.desc: Physician and educator whose classrooms let children choose hands-on work and learn at their own pace.

nodes.name: Loris Malaguzzi
nodes.desc: Founded the Reggio Emilia approach, where children's own questions drive long, collaborative projects.

nodes.name: Reggio Emilia schools
nodes.desc: Community-built early-childhood schools where learning is documented, shared, and led by children's inquiry.

nodes.name: Célestin Freinet
nodes.desc: Brought printing presses into classrooms so children could publish their own work and correspond with other schools.

nodes.name: Kurt Hahn
nodes.meta: Germany and United Kingdom · 1886–1974 · German, English
nodes.desc: Educator who believed character grows through challenge, service, and expeditions.

nodes.name: Outward Bound

nodes.name: Barefoot College

nodes.name: Schumacher College

nodes.name: EARTH University

nodes.name: John Amos Comenius
nodes.meta: Bohemia and the Netherlands · 1592–1670 · Czech, Latin
nodes.desc: His Great Didactic called for teaching all things to all people, thoroughly.

nodes.name: Paul Otlet

nodes.name: The Open University

nodes.name: Internet Archive

nodes.name: arXiv

nodes.name: Khan Academy
